title: Leading the wine program and the team
lead: The program lead's job beyond the floor: training the team, mentoring sommeliers toward the Court's levels, closing the month's numbers, and dealing with suppliers cleanly under federal rules and the Court's code.

intro.text: Four jobs, every month. Money examples here are our own round numbers, and the law described is federal only: check your state's rules too.

Compare an unfamiliar grape to one guests already know, so the server has a reference point.

lines.label: From Level 2
lines.text: COGS = beginning inventory + purchases − ending inventory, and cost % = COGS ÷ wine sales. Count the same way every time.

lines.label: Variance
lines.text: BevSpot defines variance as cost of product sold (from your POS sales) minus usage (from your counts). A negative number is product used but never sold.

know: Cost of product sold = each item's quantity sold (the POS product mix report) × its pour cost.
In BevSpot's example, $8,000 sold against $10,000 used is a $2,000 loss: 20% of usage.
Check your own count and invoices first, then pours, and only then theft.
Record deliveries against orders, and have staff log what they pull from storage.
The Court lists audits and reading inventory sheets as part of program management.

sections.name: Ethics with suppliers
sections.source: eCFR 27 CFR part 6 (tied-house) and part 10 (commercial bribery); Court of Master Sommeliers, Code of Ethics

lines.label: Federal
lines.text: The federal tied-house rules bar producers, importers and wholesalers from inducing a retailer to buy their products to the exclusion of others, with listed exceptions.

lines.label: State
lines.text: Each state has its own alcohol laws, and the federal rules never exempt anyone from them. This lesson covers the federal rules only.

know: Means to induce include giving a retailer money, equipment, signs, supplies or services, paying for advertising or display, and requiring quotas.
Samples: up to 3 liters of a wine brand per location, only if you haven't bought that brand from the supplier in the last 12 months.
A supplier may run educational seminars for your staff but may not pay their travel and lodging.
Commercial bribery: a supplier may not give a retailer's employee a bonus, prize or other thing of value to win orders.
The Court's Code of Ethics flags asking mentees to place wines you represent, in exchange for mentoring, as pay-to-play.

facts.fact: The Advanced Business of the Sommelier exam covers beverage alcohol program management, including costing, audits, list management, inventory management, staff management and training; exercises include reading and evaluating inventory sheets.
Practical preparation suggestions: continue Business of the Sommelier exercises which require staff training of theoretical understanding: what would their quiz be? How would you teach them?
Oregon State University PACE cites Gultek et al. (2006): the amount of wine training offered by restaurants was related to the quantity of wine sold.

Teach staff 'the trade before the tricks of the trade': new staff start with the basics and the inventory, learning why they do what they do, not just how. Handing off a job moves from doing it all, to micromanaging, to macromanaging, to being available when needed.

Beverage professionals taste with staff every day, spend time on viticulture and vinification, describe tannins and acid to staff over and over so they can describe them to guests, and draw comparisons from unfamiliar grapes to common ones.
A quick pour test at the start of each shift, using a graduated cylinder and an old bottle filled with water, keeps bartenders aware of pours; don't punish them for failing.

The Court of Master Sommeliers is a four-level program: Introductory Sommelier Course and Examination (in person and online), Certified Sommelier Examination (in person; only after passing the Introductory), Advanced Sommelier Course and Examination (held independently; theory written, tasting verbal, practical), Master Sommelier Diploma Examination (oral theory, deductive tasting of six wines, practical).

Mentoring guidelines: the CMS-A mission is mentoring great beverage service, not how to pass an examination; teach officially endorsed principles. Mentoring is voluntary. Fees for mentoring CMS-A exam preparation outside CMS-A courses are prohibited; reimbursement for product is acceptable. Sharing exact theory questions, service situations, blind wines or grading point weights is prohibited. Teaching to published standards is encouraged. Mentors must tell candidates that training wines and questions are a training tool, not an indication of exam content. Group mentoring is encouraged but not to be branded as official; mock examinations simulating CMS-A exams are prohibited.

Mentoring, deductive tasting: teach to the full published grid; timing candidates, sharing personal methods and noting missed areas on the grid are encouraged; sessions should not mirror exam situations exactly; sharing point weights or lists of possible wines is prohibited. Theory: asking questions from personal study and sharing study techniques is encouraged; sharing the exact curriculum examined is prohibited. Practical: critiquing service is encouraged; sharing point weights or exact service situations is prohibited.

Code of Ethics, Candidates' Bill of Rights: candidates may request mentorship and engage in a mentor-mentee relationship without fear of any expectation of reciprocity or quid pro quo. Mentoring is described as a primary responsibility of Master Sommeliers.
COGS = (BI + P) - EI; cost % = COGS ÷ wine sales.

Variance ($) = cost of product sold − usage. Usage = starting inventory − ending inventory, adding inventory received. Cost of product sold = quantity sold of each product (POS product mix report) × its pour cost. Example: usage $10,000 and cost of product sold $8,000 over a week means the bar lost 20% of its product.
Track sitting inventory in one unit of measurement, used continuously.

When variance creeps up, check in order: your own count and invoice processing first, then pour consistency (pour tests, jiggers), and theft last. Record deliveries against orders; have staff document what they remove from storage; discrepancies between pulls, par levels and on-hand stock point to problems.

27 CFR 6.21: it is unlawful for an industry member to induce a retailer to purchase its products to the exclusion of others by an interest in the retailer's license or property; by furnishing, giving, renting, lending or selling equipment, fixtures, signs, supplies, money, services or other things of value (subject to subpart D exceptions); by paying or crediting the retailer for advertising, display or distribution service; by guaranteeing loans; by credit beyond the usual period; or by requiring quotas.

27 CFR 6.1: part 6 doesn't exempt any person from State law. 6.3: part 6 applies only to transactions between industry members and retailers. 6.4(b): for malt beverages it applies only where State law imposes similar requirements.
27 CFR 6.11: industry member = producer, importer or wholesaler of distilled spirits, wine or malt beverages; retailer = anyone selling them to consumers.
27 CFR 6.91: an industry member may give a sample to a retailer who has not purchased the brand from it within the last 12 months: no more than 3 liters of any brand of wine per retail establishment.
27 CFR 6.83: product displays given or sold may not exceed $300 per brand at any one time in any one retail establishment.
27 CFR 6.88: equipment and supplies, including glassware, may be sold to a retailer at not less than the industry member's cost, with the price collected within 30 days.

27 CFR 6.94: industry members may give or sponsor educational seminars for retailers' employees, but may not pay a retailer's expenses such as travel and lodging; nominal hospitality during the event is allowed.
27 CFR 6.102: outside signs may be given or sold if they carry substantial advertising, the retailer isn't paid for displaying them, and they cost no more than $400.
27 CFR 6.152: purchasing or renting display, shelf, storage or warehouse space (slotting allowances) puts retailer independence at risk.

27 CFR 10.21: it is unlawful for an industry member to induce a trade buyer to buy its products by offering or giving a bonus, premium, compensation or other thing of value to any officer, employee or representative of the trade buyer. 10.24: sales contests offering prizes to trade buyer employees are inducements. 10.1: nothing in part 10 exempts anyone from State law.

Code of Ethics (Hospitality): a Master Sommelier asking mentees for placements of wines the MS represents in exchange for mentorship, and quid pro quo ('pay-to-play') behavior, are examples of problematic behavior. (Integrity): materially misrepresenting the quality, condition or salability of a wine for personal or professional gain is problematic; so is unethical leveraging of a business relationship to unfairly benefit a third party.

Code of Conduct: avoid compromising situations that may be seen as unacceptable business practices, and adhere to sales practices expected of a buyer or seller that do not bring the integrity of Court titles into question. A significant relationship includes a dependent professional relationship with a buyer-seller dynamic; members must recuse themselves from examining such candidates.

unverified: State alcohol laws on gifts, samples, seminars, credit and trade practices differ by state and may be stricter than federal rules; none is described, and no state's rule is presented as ours.
Whether a particular gift, dinner or trip is lawful depends on the facts and the state; the lesson states the federal rules only, not legal advice.
The Court's mentoring guidelines are written for Court members mentoring candidates; using them as a model for in-house mentoring is our recommendation, not a Court rule.
The Code of Ethics applies to Court members, candidates and those taking part in Court activities; how it bears on a non-member's buying is our reading.
The Gultek et al. (2006) training finding is cited through Oregon State University's page; the study itself was not read.
BevSpot's statement that industry shrinkage 'hovers around 20%' is not used; its 20% figure appears only as its own worked example.
The training-rhythm visual is our example plan, not a Court or trade standard.

court.outcome: Out of gratitude for the guidance that each Master Sommelier has received, some degree of mentorship is a primary responsibility that Master Sommeliers must continually endeavor to shoulder.

read.where: Each month, counts and sales become three numbers: **COGS**, **cost %** and **variance**. The Court tests the same skills: costing, **inventory sheets** and **audits**.

stops.name: COGS
stops.text: **Beginning + purchases − ending.** Example: $20,000 + $8,000 − $18,000 = **$10,000**. Divide by $40,000 in wine sales: **25%**.

stops.name: Variance
stops.text: What the POS says you sold, at cost, minus what the counts say you used. Example: $9,500 − $10,000 = **−$500**, 5% of usage.

stops.name: Find the cause
stops.text: In order: your own **count** and **invoices**, then **pours** (pour tests, jiggers), and only then **theft**.

stops.name: Audit
stops.text: Match **deliveries** to orders and log what leaves storage. Gaps between pulls, par and what's on hand show you where to look.

read.mixup: **Usage** is what your counts say you used. **Cost of product sold** is what your sales say you should have used. **Variance** is the gap.
